title: Benchmarks
lead: Reproducible recall numbers — and an unusually honest methodology.
summary: MemPalace achieves 96.6% recall@5 on LongMemEval using raw semantic search with zero API calls, demonstrating that verbatim text storage with embeddings outperforms LLM-based fact extraction. A progression to 98.4% (hybrid, held-out) and ≥99% (with LLM rerank) is achieved via keyword overlap, temporal reasoning, and preference extraction — each improvement grounded in analysis of specific failure patterns. The benchmark suite spans three academic datasets (LongMemEval, LoCoMo, ConvoMem) with published methodology, auditable result files, and a deliberate refusal to teach-to-the-test for the final 0.6%.

concepts.definition: Semantic search with ChromaDB's default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings on verbatim session text, no heuristics or LLM calls — the reproducible, offline headline result.

Two-stage ranking: semantic retrieval of top-50 candidates, then re-scoring via keyword overlap (up to 30% distance reduction for matching keywords) plus temporal proximity boost for time-anchored questions.
Optional third pass: send top-K retrieved sessions to Claude Haiku with the question; Haiku selects the most relevant session to promote to rank 1, without changing the rest of the ranking.
Clean train/test split: hybrid_v4 tuned on 50 dev questions, validated on 450 previously unseen questions to measure honest generalization (no teaching-to-the-test).

16 regex patterns detect how users express preferences in conversation ('I've been having trouble with X', 'I prefer Y'); synthetic documents bridge vocabulary gaps between question phrasing and session text.
For questions about what the assistant said: pass 1 finds top-5 sessions using user turns only; pass 2 re-indexes those sessions with full text (user + assistant) to avoid diluting the global index.

Retrieval recall measures whether the correct session is in top-K results; QA accuracy measures whether an LLM generates a correct answer. The two metrics are independent — MemPalace's 96.6% is R@5, not end-to-end accuracy.
Hybrid v4's last 0.6% (100% from 99.4%) came from analyzing three specific failed questions and building targeted fixes — teaching-to-the-test acknowledged and disclosed rather than hidden.

symbols.role: Baseline retrieval: builds a fresh MemPal palace per question, ingests all haystack sessions, queries with the question, returns ranked indices

symbols.role: Hybrid v1: semantic retrieval + keyword overlap re-ranking (two-stage)

symbols.name: build_palace_and_retrieve_hybrid_v4
symbols.role: Hybrid v4: adds quoted-phrase extraction, person-name boosting, memory/nostalgia patterns (teaching-to-the-test fix)

symbols.name: ndcg
symbols.role: Computes normalized discounted cumulative gain; metric used alongside recall@k to measure ranking quality

symbols.name: extract_keywords
symbols.role: Extracts meaningful words from text using 51-word stop list; used in hybrid re-ranking

symbols.name: keyword_overlap
symbols.role: Computes fraction of question keywords found in a document; used to compute boost score

symbols.name: extract_preferences
symbols.role: Applies 16 preference-detection regex patterns to extract how users express preferences in sessions

symbols.name: parse_time_offset_days
symbols.role: Parses temporal references like '4 weeks ago', 'last month'; returns (days_offset, tolerance_window)

symbols.role: Deletes and recreates a ChromaDB collection; called between questions to isolate state

symbols.role: Module-level EphemeralClient singleton shared across all 500 benchmark questions; eliminates memory accumulation

surprises.title: Raw text beats LLM-extracted memory by 2.1×
surprises.detail: ConvoMem shows MemPalace (92.9% average recall) vs Mem0 (30–45%). Mem0 uses an LLM to extract structured memories; MemPalace stores verbatim text. The simpler approach wins because it doesn't discard information — when an LLM extraction fails, the original text is lost, but MemPalace's embedding model can find it later. This contradicts the field's consensus that AI-powered extraction is necessary for memory systems.

surprises.title: Hybrid v1 weight 0.30 is globally optimal, not locally tuned
surprises.detail: 100-question samples showed 99% R@5 at weight 0.40, suggesting 0.40 was better. Full 500-question run reveals this was sampling variance. On all 500 questions, weights 0.30 and 0.40 are equivalent (97.8% vs 97.4%). The lesson: validate on the full dataset, not subsamples.

surprises.title: Two-pass assistant retrieval outperforms global indexing
surprises.detail: A naive fix for 'what did you say' questions is to index all turns (user + assistant) globally. This dilutes semantic signal — every session's assistant text competes with every other. The two-pass approach (find the session first using user turns, then search full text within that session) outperforms global indexing because it avoids the dilution.

surprises.title: Temporal boost maxes at 40%, not 100% — semantic matching still wins
surprises.detail: A 40% maximum reduction means excellent semantic matches cannot be completely overridden by temporal proximity. Temporal correctness is a hint, not a rule. This prevents cases where a session from the wrong time period but with perfect semantic match gets demoted below a wrong session that just happens to be from the right date.

surprises.title: The 99.4% → 100% step teaches to the test; 98.4% on unseen is the honest claim
surprises.detail: Hybrid v4's three fixes (quoted phrase, person name, nostalgia patterns) were developed by directly examining three specific failed questions. This is methodological contamination — the fixes are proven to work on those three questions, but may not generalize. The held-out evaluation of 98.4% R@5 on 450 unseen questions proves the earlier improvements (v1–v3) generalize, but v4's step remains internally contaminated. The authors disclose this rather than hiding it.

designDecisions.decision: Publish raw 96.6% as the headline, not the reranked 100%
designDecisions.rationale: The 96.6% requires no API key, no cloud, no LLM at any stage. It reproduces on a laptop in 5 minutes. This aligns with MemPalace's core pitch ('local-first, no API key'). The reranked numbers are real but require an optional LLM dependency. Publishing the harder constraint (offline, free) first, then noting the rerank as an optional upgrade, is honest and user-friendly.

designDecisions.decision: Explicit refusal to post cross-tool comparisons with Mem0, Mastra, Supermemory
designDecisions.rationale: Different systems publish different metrics on different splits. Mem0 publishes ConvoMem scores; Supermemory publishes QA accuracy (not retrieval recall); Mastra publishes QA accuracy on a different LLM. Placing R@5 next to QA accuracy is apples-to-oranges. The honest comparison requires running the same metric on the same data, which the authors did not do for other systems. Refusing to post unverified comparisons prevents misleading claims.

designDecisions.decision: Include all per-question result files in the repository, commit them, and make them auditable
designDecisions.rationale: Aggregate numbers (96.6%) without breakdown hide failure patterns. By committing JSONL files with every question, every retrieved document, and every score, MemPalace allows readers and reviewers to audit the claims. The design decision reflects the 'honest benchmarks' ethos: give people the data to verify, not just the scorecard.

designDecisions.decision: Implement train/test split (50 dev, 450 held-out) after discovering hybrid v4 teaching-to-the-test
designDecisions.rationale: Once the contamination was recognized, the authors created a clean split rather than ignoring it. This establishes a template for future work: tune on dev data (safe), publish on held-out data (final). The design acknowledges that benchmark integrity is active work, not a one-time decision.

designDecisions.decision: Cap preference extraction at 10 mentions per session to avoid overly long synthetic docs
designDecisions.rationale: Longer documents can introduce noise through false-positive embedding matches. Capping at 10 mentions (the most salient preferences) balances coverage with signal quality. The cap is documented in the code, making it reviewable.

related.why: Benchmarks validate the core retrieval claims in MemPalace's positioning and home narrative
Benchmark retrieval functions directly test the semantic search and ranking layers that power search
LLM reranking (optional) uses Claude Haiku/Sonnet; the benchmark measures how LLM reasoning bridges semantic gaps that embeddings cannot close
MCP tools support programmatic memory queries; benchmarks validate the underlying retrieval that MCP surfaces
Benchmarks ingest mined conversation data; the quality of mining affects what retrieval has to work with

searchDoc.title: Benchmarks
searchDoc.summary: MemPalace's benchmark suite reports reproducible retrieval recall on three public datasets with an unusually transparent methodology, including disclosure of where it teaches to the test.
searchDoc.body: MemPalace's benchmarks measure retrieval recall@k on three public academic datasets and document an unusually honest methodology. The headline result is 96.6 percent recall at 5 on 500 LongMemEval questions using raw semantic search: each conversation session is stored as a single document of concatenated user turns, ChromaDB embeds documents and queries with the default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer at 384 dimensions, and the top five sessions are returned by cosine similarity. This baseline needs no heuristics, no LLM, and no API key, and reproduces on a laptop in five minutes. It contradicts the assumption that AI must extract and compress memory: verbatim storage avoids the information loss of extraction, and on ConvoMem it scores 92.9 percent average recall versus Mem0's 30 to 45 percent. A four-version hybrid re-ranker layers targeted fixes on top. Hybrid v1 adds keyword overlap scoring with a 0.30 weight that reduces distance by up to 30 percent. Hybrid v2 adds temporal date parsing and proximity boosting capped at 40 percent, plus two-pass assistant retrieval that finds a session with user turns then re-indexes with full text to avoid diluting the global index. Hybrid v3 adds 16 preference-extraction regex patterns that create synthetic documents sharing the session corpus_id, capped at 10 mentions. Hybrid v4 adds quoted-phrase and person-name boosting for the final three failures, which the authors flag as teaching to the test. A clean 50 development and 450 held-out train/test split yields 98.4 percent recall at 5 on unseen data as the honest publishable number, while 100 percent comes only from tuning on the test set itself. An optional LLM rerank sends the top ten sessions to Claude Haiku, which promotes one session to rank one, costing about 0.001 dollars per query and pushing results to at least 99 percent. Across datasets MemPalace scores 96.6 percent, 98.4 percent, and at least 99 percent on LongMemEval, 88.9 percent recall at 10 on LoCoMo, 92.9 percent average on ConvoMem, and 80.3 percent recall at 5 on MemBench. Every per-question result is committed as JSONL so readers can audit failures, and the three contaminated question ids d6233ab6, 4dfccbf8, and ceb54acb are named explicitly. Key functions live in benchmarks/longmemeval_bench.py, including build_palace_and_retrieve, the hybrid v1 through v4 variants, extract_keywords, keyword_overlap, extract_preferences, parse_time_offset_days, ndcg, and a module-level EphemeralClient singleton that broke a memory wall causing crashes at question 388.
